messages.subject: distribution of variances
parts:
Hi stan-masters

I am back looking for some more wise advice. I am working on a model where I am estimating a model for each subject's time series, and from the subjects models estimate the hyper parameters to estimate the random effects. 
Here is my issue, for this model for each subject I estimate several variances, and I am not sure what would be a good distribution of variances (not the prior for the variances), I have think between a couple of options: chi-square, gamma, skew-normal.
Right now I am preferring the skew-normal, since this would allow it to account for 2 posible cases, where most variances are low and a few high, and where most are high and a few low

Thoughts about the best distribution of variances?

Thank you for advice

-- Mauricio

> On Oct 17, 2015, at 12:19 AM, Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal <mauga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi stan-masters
>
> I am back looking for some more wise advice. I am working on a model where I am estimating a model for each subject's time series, and from the subjects models estimate the hyper parameters to estimate the random effects.
> Here is my issue, for this model for each subject I estimate several variances, and I am not sure what would be a good distribution of variances (not the prior for the variances),

I don't understand what you mean by a distribution on variance
parameters that isn't a prior. Do you observe the variances somehow?

> I have think between a couple of options: chi-square, gamma, skew-normal.
> Right now I am preferring the skew-normal, since this would allow it to account for 2 posible cases, where most variances are low and a few high, and where most are high and a few low

I don't know the skew normal well enough to comment.
Are you saying that you expect one of those two possible cases
as being the only possibilities? If so, if the low and high
variances are naturally grouped, a mixture model might be
appropriate.
> Thoughts about the best distribution of variances?

That all depends on the data you're modeling!

- Bob

Hi Mauricio,

If you're actually estimating the variances then they must be parameters in your model. Any distributional assumptions you encode about them can be thought of in terms of a prior. Or maybe I'm misunderstanding your model. Can you share your Stan program? Seeing the code would make it easier for us to help.
